title: Mutable Borrows
intro: `&mut` lends a value so it can be changed. The rule: while something holds a `&mut`, nothing else can use that value at all. Many readers, or one writer, never both.

coming_from.go: `&mut Vec<i32>` is like your `*[]int`, except you don't write `(*scores)[i]`: indexing and loops look through the reference. What Go has no version of is the exclusivity: while a `&mut` exists, nothing else can read or write that value.
coming_from.kotlin: A `&mut Vec<i32>` parameter is like a `MutableList<Int>` parameter, but the caller has to write `&mut scores`, so the call shows what may change. A Kotlin `List` is a read-only view that another reference can still change under you. While a `&mut` is lent out, no other reference exists at all, not even to read.
coming_from.python: Python lets any reference change a list. Rust only allows it through `&mut`, which must be written on both the parameter and the call. Only one `&mut` can exist at a time, and nothing else can even read the list while it does.
coming_from.typescript: Any reference to an array can change it in TypeScript, unless that reference is typed `readonly`, which restricts only that one reference. In Rust only a `&mut` can change it, you write it at the call (`&mut scores`), and while it exists nothing else can read or write the value.
coming_from.java: `&mut Vec<i32>` is like passing a `List<Integer>` that the method may change, except the signature says so, and Rust allows only one such writer at a time with no readers alongside it. (A read-only view such as `Collections.unmodifiableList` exists, but it only restricts the reference you hold.) Java has references to element objects but not to a list slot, so the Rust fix for changing two elements looks like yours: `scores[i] += 1`, where you'd write `scores.set(i, scores.get(i) + 1)`.
coming_from.csharp: `&mut` is like a `ref` parameter or `ref` local, but exclusive: while one `&mut` exists, nothing else can read or write that value. C# lets two `ref` locals point at the same array slot; Rust doesn't, so use indexes or `split_at_mut`.
coming_from.c: `&mut T` is `restrict` made universal and checked. In C, `restrict` is a promise you keep yourself; Rust refuses `&mut arr[i]` and `&mut arr[j]` at once, even for different elements. (`split_at_mut` and slice patterns are the way to get two.)
coming_from.cpp: `&mut T` is a non-`const` `T&`, with one extra rule: only one can be alive at a time, and no `const` references alongside it. Two `int&` into one vector are fine in C++ (until it grows), but rejected in Rust; use indexes or `split_at_mut`.

notes: `&mut x` lends `x` out to be changed. A plain `&` only looks. Because `&mut` is written at the call, you can see which calls change your data.
`*r` means "the value `r` points at". Method calls and printing look through a reference for you, so you mostly see `*` when assigning: `*r += 1`.
You need `mut` in two places: the variable (`let mut scores`) and the borrow (`&mut scores`). The first is at the declaration, the second at the call.

This one-writer rule is the main rule that prevents data races in safe Rust, together with the `Send` and `Sync` rules for threads ([Send and Sync](/learn/send-sync/)). It is the rule of a read-write lock (many readers or one writer), but checked while compiling.

gotcha.title: Two writers into the same list
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, `first := &scores[0]; last := &scores[2]` is fine. They point at different elements, so nothing overlaps.
gotcha.rust_sees: `&mut scores[0]` lends element 0 out to be changed (see the notes above). The borrow checker does not look at index values. It sees two `&mut` borrows of `scores`, both alive at the same time. (It doesn't track indexes in an array either: there the error names `scores[_]`.)
gotcha.why: This code is safe, but Rust can't prove it. Change 0 and 2 to variables `i` and `j`. When `i == j`, you have two writers to the same number. The compiler cannot tell that case from this one, so it refuses both. When you really need two parts at once, ask for pieces that cannot overlap.

go.says: Go runs this and prints [11 20 31]. Two pointers into the same slice are fine in Go, even when both write. (If two goroutines wrote through them without coordination, that would be a data race.)

kotlin.says: Kotlin has no reference to a list slot (and an `Int` can't be changed), so you would write `scores[0] += 1` and `scores[2] += 1`. That is also the simplest Rust fix.

python.says: Python has no reference to a list slot, only to the objects in it, so you would write `scores[0] += 1` and `scores[2] += 1`. That is also the simplest Rust fix.

typescript.says: TypeScript has no reference to an array element. `let first = scores[0]; first += 1` changes a copy of the number and leaves the array alone. You would write `scores[0] += 1`, which is also the simplest Rust fix.

java.says: Java has references to element objects but not to a list slot, and an `Integer` can't be changed, so you would write `scores.set(0, scores.get(0) + 1)`. In Rust, `scores[0] += 1` is the simplest fix.

csharp.says: C# allows two `ref` locals into the same array and prints [11, 20, 31]. Nothing checks whether two refs point at the same slot.

c.says: C allows any number of pointers that write into the same array. This prints [11, 20, 31].

cpp.says: Two `int&` into the same vector are fine in C++, so this prints `[11, 20, 31]`. (They would dangle if the vector grew.) Rust allows only one `&mut` at a time, and you would use `split_at_mut` or indexes.
